content: The document outlines updated recommendations for the treatment of adolescents and children with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, as well as simplified service delivery and diagnostics for HCV. It also includes a summary of declarations of conflicts of interest from contributors to the guideline development process. 1. Conflict of Interest Declarations: The document includes a summary of significant conflicts of interest declared by members of the Guideline Development Group. These declarations are as follows: Jason Grebely: Declared research support from Cephied (USD 300,000), Gilead Sciences (USD 1,500,000), and Hologic (USD 250,000) as part of National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) Partnership Project grants. These grants involve contributions from the Australian federal government and partner organizations. Non-monetary support valued at over USD 1,000 from AbbVie (USD 5,000 in 2020), Cephied (USD 3,000 in 2020), and Gilead Sciences (USD 3,000 in 2021). Partial exclusion from voting on the HCV point-of-care viral load topic but contributed as an expert or presenter. Christian B. Ramers: Consulting for AbbVie (USD 1,500, current). Research support for a pragmatic clinical trial on mobile HCV treatment for people who inject drugs, funded by Gilead Sciences (USD 637,500). The study is investigator-led and embedded in syringe-exchange services, comparing mobile van-based care with traditional in-clinic care. The grant was received by the institution, and Ramers is not directly involved in the project or in receipt of funds. Speaker engagements for Gilead Sciences (USD 2,000, current) and AbbVie (USD 2,000, current). Declared interests were deemed not in conflict with the guideline topics. Lai Wei: Consulting for Gilead (USD 1,000 in 2020), Huahui (USD 2,000 in 2021), MSD (USD 500 in 2019), and Pfizer (USD 1,000 in 2021). Speaker engagements for Asclitis (USD 500 in 2020), BMS (USD 500 in 2018), Gilead (USD 500 in 2018, 2019, 2020), and Kayin (USD 1,000 in 2020). Research grants from AbbVie (USD 100,000 from 2017–2019 for strengthening patient management databases), BMS (USD 100,000 from 2015–2018 for HCV genotyping in China), and Gilead (USD 200,000 in 2021 for developing an algorithm to support linkage to care in 50 hospitals). Only one project is currently active, which is not linked to any specific company’s drugs. 5. Purpose of Publication: This publication is part of the WHO guideline on updated recommendations for HCV treatment and diagnostics. It is made publicly available for transparency and information purposes, in line with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014).
